Sodering
SOD-ur-ing
n. (soldering; the joining of metal with a fusible alloy — the last step in making an idol)
An older English spelling of soldering, from Old French soudure, from Latin solidare, to make solid. At Isaiah 41:7 it renders Hebrew debeq, a joining or cleaving together.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah 41 is a courtroom scene in which the LORD summons the nations to produce their gods, and He shows us instead the workshop where the gods are produced: So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved. The verse is a masterpiece of contempt achieved entirely by reporting. Four tradesmen cheer each other along; the joint is called ready; and the last act of the makers is to nail the god down so it will not fall over.

The preceding verse makes the irony explicit: They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage. The idol-makers must encourage each other because the thing they are making cannot encourage anyone. Every function a god is supposed to perform is being performed by the men in the shop — they hearten one another, they hold the work steady, they secure it against falling. The contrast in the chapter around it is total. Two verses earlier the LORD says to Israel, Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee. The idol must be fastened with nails that it be not moved; the LORD holds His people with the right hand of His righteousness.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the act of uniting metals by a fusible alloy; soldering.

expand to see more

SOLDERING, ppr. Uniting metals by a metallic cement; mending; patching up.

SOLDER, n. A metallic cement, or a metal or metallic alloy used to unite other metallic substances.

ANVIL, n. An iron block with a smooth face, on which smiths hammer and shape their work.

GOLDSMITH, n. An artisan who manufactures vessels and ornaments of gold and silver.

FASTEN, v.t. To fix firmly; to make fast or close; to secure in place.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 41:7 — "So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved."

Isaiah 41:6 — "They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, Be of good courage."

Isaiah 44:17 — "And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god."

Habakkuk 2:18 — "What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?"

Modern Corruption

Idolatry is imagined as belief in a statue, when Isaiah shows it as a social project — men encouraging one another around a thing they all know they made.

expand to see more

The workshop in Isaiah 41 is a picture of manufactured consensus. Nobody in that shop is deceived about where the god came from; they watched it being hammered. What holds the whole thing up is that they say Be of good courage to each other while they work. This is the social mechanism of every idolatry, including the modern varieties: what makes a thing credible is not evidence but the fact that everyone in the shop is nodding, and the nodding has to be constantly maintained because the object cannot maintain itself. Habakkuk names the idol a teacher of lies, and this is the lesson it teaches — that a thing enough people affirm together must be real.

The believer's protection is not scepticism but the contrast the chapter itself draws. The idol must be nailed down that it be not moved; the LORD says to His servant, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness. One is secured by its makers; the other secures His people. Where a Christian finds himself needing constant reassurance from others that a thing is so, it is worth asking which side of Isaiah 41 he is standing on — the shop where the courage is passed around, or the covenant where it is given from outside.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew debeq (H1694), a joining or solder; paam (H6471), an anvil or stroke; charash (H2796), a craftsman.

expand to see more

Hebrew debeq (H1694) — a joining, solder; from dabaq, to cleave or cling.

Hebrew paam (H6471) — a stroke, and so the anvil; the block struck in the shop.

Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine, to smelt; the goldsmith's trade.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to strengthen, to encourage; used both of the workmen and of the LORD to Israel.

Hebrew masmer (H4548) — a nail; what keeps the god upright.

Usage

"“It is ready for the sodering” — four tradesmen cheering each other on."

"“he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved” — a god secured by its makers."

"“They helped every one his neighbour” — the courage the idol could not supply."
